I tracked every single purchase I made for a full year by writing it in a notebook by hand and it genuinely rewired how I think about money
Other
This started as kind of a dare to myself. I'd tried every budgeting app out there and they all felt like checking a score after a game I'd already lost. YNAB, Mint, a spreadsheet phase that lasted eleven days. The problem was always the same: the friction was too low. Tap, pay, done, forgotten. So sometime in late 2021 I bought a cheap narrow notebook that fit in my back pocket and made one rule every transaction gets written down within two minutes of happening, by hand, with a pen, no exceptions.

The first two weeks were uncomfortable in a way I didn't expect. Not because it was hard to do, but because writing "$6.60, iced coffee" in ink while standing on the sidewalk made me feel something. Mild embarrassment maybe, or just the sensation of a decision becoming real instead of evaporating into a phone screen. By month two I noticed I was making fewer impulsive purchases not because I was restricting myself but because the mental preview of having to write something down was enough to make me pause. By month six my savings rate had gone up considerably without me setting a single hard limit on any category. I finished the full year. Went through four notebooks total. The last pge of the fourth one I just wrote the number I had managed to save that year and closed it. I'm not saying this works for everyone and I get that it sounds kind of unhinged. But there's something about analog accountability that apps genuinely can not replicate the physical act of recording a choice makes it feel like a choise, not just a transaction.

I've always said... "If you can't measure it, you can't manage it".

I'd tried every budgeting app out there and they all felt like checking a score after a game I'd already lost.

With YNAB and other zero-sum/envelope-style budgeting systems, the magic is in the process of giving every dollar a job. You think ahead and allocate all your dollars to the categories (ie. jobs) where they will be needed. Then you spend from those categories, not from your account balances. If using YNAB felt like you were checking a score after a game you already lost, I suspect you weren't using it as it was intended.

The problem was always the same: the friction was too low. Tap, pay, done, forgotten.

I've never heard this one before. Usually people don't stick with something because of too much friction. No matter which method you use, you have to do it and stay engaged with it, or it becomes meaningless.

I was a YNAB'er for MANY years (since 2007), and switched to Actual Budget early last year. Both work about the same. But the idea behind envelope budgeting is that you spend according to your budget categories. I got in the habit of entering every transaction manually very shortly after point-of-sale. Very similar to your pen & paper method, I'd pull out my phone, open YNAB (now Actual Budget), and manually enter the transaction. It was always before driving away from the gas pump, before leaving the table at the restaurant, while standing on the sidewalk outside the store, or immediately after ordering something online.

But the real secret was... BEFORE spending money, you open up the app and check the balance for each category you're about to spend from. If there's money there, you're golden. If not, you have some decisions to make. Either don't spend, or steal money from other categories.

Rebuilding my finances from zero after a divorce at 32, my tracking system
Credit
Got divorced last year. went from dual-income with $75k combined savings to a studio apartment with $10k and a car payment. sharing the system i built because posts here about budgeting tend to assume you already have a foundation. sometimes you're building from scratch.

Budgeting: YNAB. resisted it for years because of the subscription. $99/year is nothing compared to what i was losing. first month i found $315 in forgotten subscriptions. ""give every dollar a job"" forced intentionality in a way spreadsheets never did.

Savings: Some Bank. separate buckets for emergency fund, car maintenance, and annual expenses. the psychological separation matters even though it's technically one account.

Net worth tracking: Google Sheets. updated on the 1st of every month, one row per month, columns for each account. graphing total net worth and watching the line go up slowly is the most motivating thing i've found. $10k to $28k in the first year.

Check-ins: Willow Voice. every two weeks on payday i talk through how the last pay period went. skim the transcript and adjust YNAB categories if needed. reading back early entries versus recent ones is genuinely encouraging.

Investing: not there yet. building the 6-month emergency fund first. then Roth IRA, target-date index funds. keeping it simple.

The hardest part about rebuilding after a major life event is the psychological weight. you KNOW what to do. doing it when you're emotionally drained requires systems that work on autopilot.

anyone else rebuild from a major financial reset? what worked for you?

I tracked my spending for the past 4 months and I am spending around $1,300 per month on food/groceries. I am feeling so angry and disappointed. How to fix this?
Budgeting
I am actually ashamed about this.

I'm a 31 year old single woman. I moved to Canada from the middle east 4.5 years ago. My income for the first four years was very minimal, around $2,200 per month as a PhD student and teaching assistant. I could barely save anything, and I thought that was normal. Turns out, I was just lazy and spoiled, splurging like I was rich.

I got a job a few months ago. My take home is a little over $4,000. I tracked the past 4 months of my spending and noticed that I am routinely going over $1,800 a month and ~$1,200- $1,400 of it is Restaurants and Grocery. I basically never cook at home. I don't go to shop for groceries, only get them from Instacart and similar apps. Doordash, UberEats and Instacart. Weekly. Sometimes every single day of the week... and I tip, too. Always.

This is disgusting. I can't help but do the math...Let's say a normal person spends ~$500 on groceries a month (that's what my friend does, he never eats out). I would have been able to save $800- $1,200 that way. That is over $42,000 for the last 4 and a half years. That's 2 years worth of rent for a 1 bedroom apartment.

I feel so angry at myself for this. I immediately removed UberEats, Doordash and Instacart. I locked my Credit Card. I will transfer $3,600 of my pay to a savings account and use the rest for rent. I will not be buying food for the next 3 months. I will only buy something if I go there in person and shop for it. Since I don't have a car, that means I would have to buy very few items. Otherwise, I will use whatever I have at home.

I'm terrified and ashamed and shocked at this. I don't know what to do. I've never been taught how to be an adult. Growing up, the one thing I was told was "you're gonna get married and some man is going to take care of you so you don't need to know this"... and I somehow internalized that, despite doing my best to not get married and not be dependent on anyone else. I'm not starving. I have some money saved up (a lot less than the 40k)... but I can't stop thinking about that.

Especially because I was looking forward to moving out of the place I've been living in: a student housing with 4 other girls, almost all of whom are undergraduates. Now I feel like I have to punish myself by staying here (but I'm already paying way too much, almost $1,200 for this). Please help. I need to know how to fix this and stop spending like I'm rich because I'm definitely not. I need to learn how to budget. I need to know if it's a good idea to move. It is for my sanity and self-esteem, but is that financially the right move? Especially now that I know I've wasted so much money?

I'm so freaked out, I was thinking of applying for second jobs... I don't know how to move past this.

Oh my gosh - I can hear the shame in your text. It’s ok!!! This is how we learn!!!! You’re learning!!! Be gentle with yourself!!!

You may still need instacart or something similar for grocery delivery. That’s not weakness that’s using your resources. Decide on 2 breakfast options (something that takes a few minutes, and something fast and easy). Then decide what 2 meals you can cook this week. Make enough that you have leftovers of each. That’s 4-5 dinners. For lunch, I’m a sucker for a bean salad. I get so much fiber that way. But pick one or two lunches for the week. Make extra.

My goodness.

First, kudos to you for examining your spending. Most of us are not very good at that. I understand the negative feelings, but I think in time you will look back on this as an overall positive in your life.

How to budget? There are a lot of tools out there, and I cant pretend to know the best one overall, or the one that will wok best for you specifically. You have done the first important steps. Identify your income. Look at your spending for the past 6 months. Identify average monthyl expenditures. Divide costs into fixed and variable. Commonly Food, Housing, Car, would be fixed costs. Other expenses like, Clothing, Entertainment (which would be restaurants, etc) , credit card interest, etc. etc. etc are more easily to reduce. There's a sweet spot between so few categories that the data is meaningless and so many categories that trends are impossible to spot. In general anything that is more than 10% of your expenses deserves it's own category.

The next step is hard--if you have a negative between earned and expended you have to reduce expenses. usually the variable costs are easiest to reduce. If that is niot adequate then is when you have to consider moving to a smaller place, selling your car, or other drastic measures....

If you have a positive delta--you make more than you spend each month--then you still have the opportunity to examine your spedning and decide if what you spend money on is more important to you then savings.....

It's good that you've learned this and yourself and are committed to fix it, but maybe pause before you take extreme action:

Do you know how to cook?

Do you have time to cook?

It's pretty normal to get into weird self-care habits when you're doing something as intense as a Masters/PhD program.

Also, the idea that eating out is inherently wasteful is fallacious and doesn't match with history or the many many poor people who can only afford to eat out in parts of the world where they can't afford a kitchen.

It's good that you've found a hole in your wallet and you're trying to change, but viewing yourself as capital B bad because you made a mistake is not likely to help you long term.

when people shame themselves into doing things, what they're doing is imagining painful situations and associating the bad behavior with base lizard-brain pain response. "If I don't do the dishes people will think I'm gross and then I'll be alone".

But sometimes the pain isn't associated with the behavior you want to avoid, but with the whole topic, so when you think about doing the dishes at all, you start freaking out.

But you can do this in reverse. You can come up with several big goals you have that, when you think about achieving them, you feel a warm, fuzzy feeling like pride or a hug. You dwell on them until you can feel that satisfaction. This is a pleasure response, just as powerful as but opposite to the fear response. You associate the habit you need to build with one of those goals. One of my goals is to be a great host. So instead of shame, I can think "If I do the dishes, everything will be nice and clean and everything will go smoothly".
